Series::asinh¶

Back to Series API Reference

Signature¶

Series::asinh() const -> Series

What It Does¶

asinh() applies the inverse hyperbolic sine elementwise. It recovers y from x=sinh(y) and is defined for every finite real input.

An Unbounded Inverse With Logarithmic Growth¶

Unlike asin(), asinh() has no [-1,1] restriction. Hyperbolic sine maps the whole real line onto the whole real line, so its inverse does the same. asinh() is odd, passes through zero, behaves approximately like x near zero, and grows only logarithmically at large magnitude.

Those properties make it useful for compressing signed heavy-tailed data while preserving sign and retaining more detail around zero than a blunt clipping operation.

Parameters¶

None. Every element is transformed independently and shape is preserved.

Returns¶

Series A new Series of inverse-hyperbolic values. Integral, bool, and float8 inputs promote to floating output rather than truncating fractional values.

Gradient¶

d asinh(x) / dx = 1 / sqrt(1 + x^2)

The derivative equals one at zero and smoothly decreases toward zero as the input magnitude grows. It is finite everywhere on the real line.

Examples¶

Example 1. Known sinh() values recover -1, 0, and 1.

auto values = pluss::make_series({
    -1.1752011936438014,
    0.0,
    1.1752011936438014,
});
std::cout << values.asinh() << "\n";

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[-1, 0, 1]

Example 2. Integral input promotes instead of losing the fractional result.

auto integers = pluss::make_series({-1, 0, 1}, pluss::ScalarType::Int64);
std::cout << integers.asinh() << "\n";

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=float32, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[-0.88137358, 0, 0.88137358]

Example 3. Reverse mode is strongest near zero and weaker away from it.

auto x = pluss::make_series({0.0, 0.75});
x.tracks_slope_(true);
x.asinh().sum().reverse();
std::cout << x.sensitivity() << "\n";

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[2], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=2, contiguous=true)
data=[1, 0.8]

Gotchas And Failure Modes¶

  • asinh() and asin() are different functions; only asin() has a bounded real input domain and returns an angle.

  • Large magnitudes are compressed, so equal output differences do not represent equal input differences.

  • The method is out-of-place; asinh_() is the mutating sibling.

Summary¶

Use asinh() for an invertible, sign-preserving compression of unrestricted real values. It is smooth over the complete real line and promotes integral input to floating output.

See Also¶

  • Series::sinh: forward hyperbolic sine.

  • Series::acosh: inverse hyperbolic cosine with domain x>=1.

  • Series::atanh: inverse hyperbolic tangent with domain |x|<=1.
